stem: Under Article III, Section 12 of the 1987 Constitution, a person under investigation for an offense has the right to remain silent and to have counsel. How may he give up (waive) these rights?
choices: By telling the investigating officer so out loud
In writing, even if no lawyer is present
Only in writing and in the presence of counsel
In writing, before any public officer he chooses
answer: Only in writing and in the presence of counsel
hints: Section 12 sets two conditions for a valid waiver. A choice that meets only one of them is wrong.
Recall the last sentence of the first paragraph of Section 12. It begins: "These rights cannot be waived except..."
Ask of each choice: is it in writing? Is counsel (a lawyer) there? Keep only the choice where both are true.

solution.methodName: Recall the exact words of the provision

steps.action: Find the provision: Article III, Section 12(1) of the 1987 Constitution.
It gives a person under investigation "the right to be informed of his right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel preferably of his own choice".
Then it says: "These rights cannot be waived except in writing and in the presence of counsel."
steps.why: To waive a right means to give it up. The word "and" means both conditions are needed.

steps.action: A spoken waiver fails (not in writing). A written waiver without a lawyer fails (no counsel). Another public officer is not counsel.
The answer is: only in writing and in the presence of counsel.

trapNotes.By telling the investigating officer so: A spoken waiver is not "in writing". Section 12 needs writing and counsel.
trapNotes.In writing, even if no lawyer is present: Writing alone is not enough. Section 12 also requires "the presence of counsel".
trapNotes.In writing, before any public officer he: Section 12 requires counsel, meaning a lawyer, to be present. Any other public officer does not count.
